## Data

Records were split by species: *known* species appear in training, while *novel* species are held out entirely, so their scores show how the model handles species it has never seen. Novel-species records with a near-copy (99% identity or more) in training were found with VSEARCH; *clean* records have none, and are the honest measure.

Training samples were capped at 2,000 records per class (validation: 200), spread across as many species as possible. Classes with under 20 records were left out (1 of them), and 7 validation records with a near-copy in training were removed.

| Sample | Records | Classes | Species per class |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training | 90 | 2 | 12 |
| Validation, known species | 90 | 2 | 12 |

## Training

3 candidate models were compared on the validation samples (never the test sets), and the best was chosen by the mean macro-F1 across them. Each training record also gave 1 random fragment of 75-600 bases, so the model learns short inputs too. Every candidate is recorded in MLflow (run `train-run`).

| Validation set | Accuracy | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| Known species | 97.0% | 0.890 |
| Novel species | 97.0% | 0.890 |
| Known species, fragments | 97.0% | 0.890 |
| Novel species, fragments | 97.0% | 0.890 |

## Calibration

Confidence was corrected with a temperature that depends on length, T = exp(-0.2810 - 0.0090 * ln(length)), fitted on the validation samples (whole sequences and new random fragments). It changes only confidence, never the prediction. *ECE* (expected calibration error) is the average gap between confidence and accuracy; 0 is perfect.

| Validation set | Accuracy | Mean confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Validation, novel species | 97.0% | 92.0% → 96.8% | 0.040 → 0.006 |

## Test results

Measured once, on test sets the model and its selection never saw. *Accuracy* counts every record equally; *macro-F1* gives every class equal weight, so rare groups count as much as common ones.

| Test set | Records | Accuracy | Top-5 | Macro-F1 | Confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Known species | 1,000 | 97.0% | 99.0% | 0.890 | 96.8% | 0.006 |
| Novel species (clean) | 1,000 | 97.0% | 99.0% | 0.890 | 96.8% | 0.006 |

6 test records had no group or order label, and 2 belonged to classes too rare to train on; these were not scored.

## Can the confidence be trusted?

Each point is a group of predictions with similar confidence; on the diagonal, confidence matches how often the model is right.

![Reliability chart](marker-reliability.svg)

Accepting only predictions at or above a confidence threshold (novel species (clean)):

| Threshold | Share accepted | Accuracy of those |
|---|---|---|
| 90% | 94.0% | 99.7% |

## Hardest classes

The 10 classes with the lowest F1 on novel species (clean), among those with at least 20 test records. *Precision*: of the records predicted as this class, the share that were; *recall*: of this class's records, the share found.

| Class | Records | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rare | 25 | 0.500 | 0.400 | 0.440 |
| Diptera | 500 | 0.990 | 0.980 | 0.985 |

## Limitations

- **Short sequences** are much less accurate (at 100 bases, 97% accurate on novel species (clean)); below 100 bases they are declined.
- **Rare classes** have few reference records, so their scores vary more (see *Hardest classes*). Classes too rare to train on are never predicted.
- **The reference data reflects what has been sequenced**: GenBank holds far more records for some groups and regions than others, and some records are misidentified.
- **Confidence** is calibrated on validation data like the test data; on sequences unlike the reference data (contaminated, chimeric, or from a poorly sampled group) it may be too high.
